procedural_history.impugned_order: Implicitly, the charge sheet and cognizance order of the Sessions Judge, Rampur, are being challenged, though indirectly through challenging the maintainability of the second petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. First Petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. (Criminal Misc. Application No. 8465 of 2018) before the Allahabad High Court: The petitioner challenged the Government's sanction order dated 03.12.2013. The High Court disposed of the application on 15.12.2020, granting liberty to the petitioner to approach the Trial Court and challenge the sanction order.
2. A quash petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. was dismissed on 28.01.1995 and without mentioning the same, another petition was filed under Section 482 Cr.P.C. with a similar prayer.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner approached the Supreme Court via a Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No. 7976 of 2023. The Supreme Court dismissed the Special Leave Petition, finding it devoid of merit. The core issue was whether a second petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is maintainable on grounds that were available for challenge at the time of filing the first petition. The Supreme Court held that it is not, especially when the charge sheet and cognizance were already on record before the first petition was filed.

decision.appeal_result: The Special Leave Petition is devoid of merit and is accordingly dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Is a second petition maintainable under Section 482 Cr.P.C. on grounds that were available for challenge even at the time of filing of the first petition thereunder?

facts: A petitioner was accused in a criminal case, and after investigation, a charge-sheet was filed and cognizance was taken by the court.
In 2018, the petitioner filed a first petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C., but only challenged the government's sanction to prosecute.
This first petition was disposed of.
In 2022, the petitioner filed a second petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C., this time challenging the charge-sheet and the cognizance order.
The grounds for challenging the charge-sheet and cognizance order were already available to the petitioner when the first petition was filed in 2018.
law: There is no absolute or "blanket rule" that a second petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is never maintainable. Its admissibility depends on the facts and circumstances of the case.
A second petition may be allowed in cases of "changed circumstances" or if new facts justify it.
However, a person is not permitted to raise pleas one after another in successive petitions if all such pleas were available to them at the time of the first petition.
Filing petitions with "instalment pleas" is considered an abuse of the legal process, as it can be used by an accused to stall proceedings.
application: The Court observed that the charge-sheet and the cognizance order, which were the subject of the second petition, existed well before the petitioner filed the first petition.
The petitioner had the opportunity to challenge the charge-sheet and cognizance in the first petition but chose to challenge only the sanction order.
By filing a second petition on grounds that were available earlier, the petitioner was attempting to raise pleas in instalments.
The Court reasoned that allowing this would enable an accused to abuse the process of law and effectively stall the criminal proceedings against them.
The Court agreed with the principle that a petitioner must raise all available pleas at the first instance and cannot withhold some to file another petition later.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the second petition was not maintainable. It was rejected because the petitioner was raising grounds that were available for challenge at the time of the first petition. The Court held that a litigant cannot invoke the court's jurisdiction repeatedly by raising pleas in instalments, as this constitutes an abuse of the legal process designed to stall proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Is a second petition maintainable under Section 482 Cr.P.C. on grounds that were available for challenge even at the time of filing of the first petition thereunder?
appellant_arguments: A second petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is maintainable.
respondent_arguments: The petitioner was not at liberty to again invoke the inherent jurisdiction of the High Court to challenge the charge sheet and the cognizance order, as the filing of the charge sheet and the cognizance thereof occurred well before the filing of the first petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. (which only challenged the sanction order).

cases.case_name: Superintendent and Remembrancer of Legal Affairs, West Bengal vs. Mohan Singh and others
cases.principle: A subsequent application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is maintainable if it is based on changed circumstances and is not a repeat application on the exact same facts.

cases.case_name: Anil Khadkiwala vs. State (Government of NCT of Delhi) and another
cases.principle: Affirms the principle that a subsequent application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is maintainable if it is not a repeat application squarely on the same facts and circumstances as the first.

cases.case_name: S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. vs. Neeta Bhalla and another
cases.principle: When a first petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is withdrawn with liberty to avail other legal remedies, the High Court is not prevented from exercising its inherent jurisdiction if petitioned again.

cases.case_name: Vinod Kumar, IAS. vs. Union of India and others
cases.principle: The dismissal of an earlier petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. does not bar the filing of a subsequent petition under the same section if the facts justify it.

cases.case_name: Simrikhia vs. Dolley Mukherjee and Chhabi Mukherjee and another
cases.principle: A second petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is not maintainable if it is based on facts that already existed at the time of the first petition, as the High Court does not have the power to review or upset its own prior order which has attained finality.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A second petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not maintainable when it raises pleas that were available to be raised at the time of the first petition. An aggrieved person cannot invoke the inherent jurisdiction of the High Court to raise one plea after another in successive petitions if all such pleas were available at the first instance.
obiter: There is no blanket rule that a second petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would not lie in any situation; its maintainability depends upon the facts and circumstances of the individual case.
A subsequent application under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would be maintainable in changed circumstances.
Dismissal of an earlier petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would not bar the filing of a subsequent petition thereunder if the facts so justify.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While there is no absolute bar on filing a second petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C., it is not permissible for an aggrieved person to raise pleas in a subsequent petition that were available to them at the time of the first petition. A second petition is only maintainable if it is based on changed circumstances or facts that developed after the disposal of the initial petition.
legal_tests_applied: A subsequent application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is maintainable in changed circumstances, provided it is not a repeat application squarely on the same facts and circumstances that existed at the time of the first petition.
why_appellant_lost: The grounds for the second petition, namely the challenge to the charge sheet and the cognizance order, were already in existence and available to the petitioner when the first petition (which only challenged the sanction order) was filed.

The petitioner was not at liberty to again invoke the inherent jurisdiction of the High Court in relation to the charge sheet and the cognizance order at a later point of time, as these were not new developments or changed circumstances arising after the first petition was decided.
why_respondent_won: The respondent correctly argued that the filing of the charge sheet and the cognizance thereof occurred well before the filing of the first petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C., and therefore, the petitioner could not challenge them in a second, subsequent petition.
The court agreed that since the pleas were available at the first instance, the petitioner was not at liberty to again invoke the inherent jurisdiction of the High Court for those same matters.
policy_considerations: Permitting the ﬁling of successive petitions u/s. 482 Cr.P.C. ignoring this principle would enable an ingenious accused to eﬀectively stall the proceedings against him to suit his own interest and convenience, by ﬁling one petition after another u/s. 482 Cr.P.C., irrespective of when the cause therefor arose.
Allowing such successive petitions on grounds that were previously available constitutes an abuse of process which cannot be permitted.
